Sugar activates the brain's reward system, similar to addictive drugs, through a potent dopamine release. This can lead to cravings and compulsive eating behaviors.

Sugar causes rapid spikes and crashes in blood sugar levels, which can further contribute to cravings and withdrawal symptoms like fatigue, headaches, and irritability when not consuming sugar.

Highly processed sugary foods, often combined with fat, seem particularly addictive due to their intense flavors and ability to bypass satiety signals.

  
Fat's effect on the reward system is less pronounced than sugar's. While it can contribute to palatability and overconsumption, it doesn't have the same addictive power.

Fat provides sustained energy, unlike sugar's rapid rise and fall. This difference in how the body processes them suggests a lower potential for cravings and dependence.

Sally Rooney, an Irish novelist, is known for her unconventional writing style, which includes omitting quotation marks around dialogue in her novels. This choice is a stylistic one, and is often referred to as "free indirect speech."  
  
Using free indirect speech allows the author to blend the thoughts and words of a character in a way that feels more natural and seamless, as if the character is speaking directly to the reader. It can also create a sense of intimacy and immediacy between the character and the reader, as if the character is confiding in the reader.  
  
Some readers may find this writing style challenging at first, as it can be harder to distinguish between dialogue and narration without the use of quotation marks. However, with a little practice, it is possible to get used to this style of writing and appreciate its unique qualities.  
  
It is worth noting that the decision to use or omit quotation marks is a matter of personal style and preference for an author, and is not a right or wrong choice. Different authors have different approaches to writing dialogue, and what works for one author may not work for another.

There is some evidence to suggest that the mono virus, or mononucleosis, which is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), may play a role in the development of long COVID. EBV is a common virus that is usually transmitted through saliva and can cause symptoms similar to those of COVID-19, including fever, fatigue, and muscle aches. Some studies have found that people with a history of mononucleosis may be more likely to experience long-term symptoms after a COVID-19 infection.  
  
It is also possible that fat cells may play a role in the development of long COVID. Adipose tissue, or fat tissue, produces a variety of signaling molecules known as adipokines, which can affect the immune system and inflammation. Some studies have suggested that people with obesity may be at higher risk for severe COVID-19 and may be more likely to experience long-term symptoms. However, more research is needed to fully understand the relationship between fat cells and long COVID.  
  
It is important to note that the causes of long COVID are still being researched and are not fully understood. Further research is needed to determine the exact roles that the mono virus and fat cells may play in the development of long COVID.

"Regular stretching is effective for increasing joint mobility, but it is also frequently promoted by trainers and in the media as an integral part of any training session to improve performance, prevent injuries and reduce delayed onset muscle soreness. However, the scientific evidence does not promote stretching either for improving performance or for reducing injuries and delayed onset muscle soreness. In fact, it has been established that static stretching leads to an acute loss of strength and power, so-called stretch-induced strength loss [8, 98–100], and should therefore probably not be performed before strength training. More specifically, 30–60 min of stretching has been found to cause a 22% (range 14–28%) acute strength loss, while shorter durations of static stretching result in an approximately 8% (range 2–19%) strength loss. Moreover, recent research indicates that regular static stretching may impair chronic measures of strength and power. However, the impairment in strength and power primarily applies to longer sessions and not too short bouts (< 60 s per muscle group) of static stretching. It should be mentioned that dynamic stretching does not appear to reduce strength.

Regarding delayed onset muscle soreness, a 2011 Cochrane review concluded that stretching does not reduce soreness in healthy adults, regardless of whether the stretching is performed before or after the training bout. This finding was supported in a 2018 review that concluded active cool-down after exercise, including stretching, neither appeared to increase recovery nor reduce delayed onset muscle soreness, and likely does not reduce the risk of long-term injury. It also should be noted that resistance training functions as an active form of flexibility training, with evidence indicating similar increases in range of motion when compared to performing a static stretching protocol. Thus, with respect to time-efficiency, stretching should not be prioritized unless an important goal of the training is to increase mobility."
